title: Transient asystole associated with vasovagal reflex in an oral surgery patient: A case report
case_prompt:
A 38-year-old woman with pronounced dental phobia but no needle phobia was scheduled for extraction of her left mandibular third molar under intravenous sedation. She reported occasional brief fainting episodes in daily life that resolved within seconds when lying supine; these events were never evaluated with central nervous system or cardiac studies. She had no personal or family history of cardiovascular disease or sudden cardiac death, and routine physical examinations and physician consultations were unremarkable.

Preoperative laboratory studies, including blood biochemistry, were normal. A screening ECG showed normal sinus rhythm at 69 bpm. After topical application of 18 mg lidocaine patch for 30 minutes, an intravenous line was placed with minimal pain under noninvasive blood pressure monitoring (118/76 mmHg) and lead II ECG (73 bpm). The patient showed no signs of hypovolemia or dehydration but received lactated Ringer’s solution.

Immediately after cannulation, she complained of discomfort and nausea. The ECG tracing revealed a progression from severe sinus bradycardia (<30 bpm) to transient asystole lasting 18 seconds, accompanied by loss of consciousness and a brief convulsion. Preparations for resuscitation were in place, but within seconds of administering oxygen, additional fluid loading, and positioning supine with elevation of the lower extremities, her rhythm recovered to an atrioventricular junctional rhythm, and she regained consciousness (blood pressure 111/67 mmHg; heart rate 75 bpm).
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Cardiogenic arrhythmia was considered unlikely because the patient “had no past or family medical history responsible for asystole relevant to cardiovascular diseases … and had no problems in regular physical examinations.”  
2. Hypovolemia or orthostatic hypotension was excluded as there were “no clinical signs of hypovolemia or dehydration suggesting an indication for administration of Ringer’s solution before the emergency.”  
3. Vasovagal reflex was deemed the cause given the temporal relation to venipuncture and characteristic findings: “ECG showed the change from serious bradycardia below 30 bpm to transient asystole for 18 s associated with VVR.”  
4. The Bezold–Jarisch reflex mechanism supported the diagnosis, as this reflex “gives rise to hypotension, bradycardia, or cardiac arrest due to VVR” in response to painful or psychological stress.
